LESSONS.title: Errors, revisited
LESSONS.goal: Guess what went wrong from an error's name
summary: The error's name is your clue
ValueError, ZeroDivisionError and more
KeyError and TypeError: the name is a hint too

cards.say: When an error happens, its name shows up on the last line. That name is your clue! The code below is fine, but scores[2] would give an IndexError, and 10 / 0 a ZeroDivisionError.
The same code can work or crash depending on the input. 3 is fine, but 0 gives a ZeroDivisionError. You can never predict what people will type!

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.code:
n = int("abc")
print(n)
items.explain: int() can only convert strings that look like numbers. A value with the wrong shape, like "abc", gives a ValueError.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.code: print(10 / 0)
items.explain: You can't divide by 0, so it's a ZeroDivisionError. The name says exactly what happened: “zero division error”. Easy to read!

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.code:
scores = [70, 80, 90]
print(scores[3])
items.explain: The list only has indexes 0, 1 and 2. Asking for index 3, which doesn't exist, gives an IndexError.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.code:
menu = {"coffee": 3000}
print(menu["tea"])
items.explain: Asking a dictionary for a key it doesn't have, like "tea", gives a KeyError. A bad index in a list is an IndexError; a bad key in a dictionary is a KeyError.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.code: print("Age: " + 20)
items.explain: You can't join a string and a number with +. The types don't match, so it's a TypeError. Turn the number into a string with str() and they'll join.

items.q: Fill in the blank so this shows 13 with no error.
items.code:
n = int(___)
print(n + 1)
items.explain: "12" looks like a number, so int() converts it. int() can't read "twelve" or "1.5", so those give a ValueError.

items.task: Read a and b with input() (leave the parentheses empty) and convert them with int(). If b is 0, print “Can't divide”; otherwise print a / b. Example: entering 10 and 4 prints 2.5
hints: Only the case where b is 0 is handled differently. Which case are the example's 10 and 4?
You can stop an error before it happens with an if. Remember if and else from Chapter 3.
First check whether b is 0. If it is, print the message; if not, print the result of the division.
items.explain: You checked whether b is 0 with an if first, so the ZeroDivisionError never happens. It also handles 0 as the first number (0 / 5 is fine). In the next lesson, we'll catch errors directly.

items.q: What does the name ValueError tell you?
options: The value has the wrong shape
items.explain: A ValueError means the type is right but the value's shape is wrong. A missing name is a NameError, and bad indentation is an IndentationError.

LESSONS.title: Catching errors
LESSONS.goal: Catch errors with try and except and keep running
summary: An error inside try jumps to except
No error? except is skipped
Write the error name after except
Put try inside while True to ask again

cards.say: If an error happens inside try, Python stops right there and jumps to except. Instead of crashing with a clue, it shows our own message, and the program keeps going.
If there's no error, the whole except block is skipped. And always write the error name, like except ValueError. A bare except swallows every clue and hides the real cause.
Want to keep asking until the answer is right? Put try inside while True. On success, break leaves the loop; on failure, except shows a message and we go back to the top.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: int("abc") raises a ValueError, so Python jumps straight to except. “Got it” never prints; only “Not a number” does.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 7 looks like a number, so there's no error. With no error, the except block is skipped and only “Got it” prints.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: A was already printed before the error. B, below the line with the error, never runs; Python goes straight to C in except.

items.q: Fill in the blank so entering abc shows the message.
items.explain: int("abc") raises a ValueError. With a different name, the error isn't caught and you get the clue as usual.

items.q: Put the lines in order so entering 7 shows 8, then Done.
items.explain: try comes first and holds the risky work, then except follows. The last print has no indentation, so it always runs.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: x and y both raise a ValueError in int(), so “Again” prints twice and the loop goes on. Only the third input, 3, reaches break, and then 3 is printed.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the loop ends once a valid number comes in.
items.explain: You need break to leave while True on success. With continue or pass the loop never ends, and once the input runs out you get a clue.

items.task: Read an age with input() (leave the parentheses empty), convert it with int() and store it in n. If it's not a number, print “Please enter a number”; if it is, print “Age next year: N”. Catch it with except ValueError. Example: 20 gives Age next year: 21
hints: The output depends on whether it's a number. Which side is 3.5 on?
Put the line that might fail inside try, and write that error's name after except.
Put the int() line and the print that uses n inside try. Put the message in except.
items.explain: You caught only int()'s ValueError, by name. int() can't read 3.5, so it shows the message, and 0 is an edge case that still works fine.

items.q: What goes wrong if you write just except: with no error name?
options: It swallows every error and hides the cause
items.explain: A bare except quietly swallows the clues from typos and other bugs too. Name the error you want to catch, and the other clues stay alive.

LESSONS.title: Handling several errors
LESSONS.goal: Use several excepts, plus else and finally
summary: You can write one except per error
else runs only with no error; finally always runs
Specific excepts first, Exception last

cards.say: To show a different message for each error, write several excepts. Python checks from the top and runs only the first match. Not a number → ValueError; dividing by 0 → ZeroDivisionError.
else runs only when there's no error. finally always runs at the end, error or not. Exception catches almost every error, so put it last.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The second input, abc, raises a ValueError. The first except matches, so only that one runs.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: 7 causes no error, so B in else runs. C in finally always runs, error or not.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: x raises a ValueError, so A prints and else is skipped. C in finally runs this time too.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: With Exception first, the ZeroDivisionError gets caught there. The except below never gets a turn, so put the specific one on top.

items.q: Fill in the blank so a missing index shows the message.
items.explain: A missing list index is an IndexError. KeyError is for dictionary keys and ValueError is for a value's shape, so they wouldn't catch this.

items.q: Put the lines in order so entering 5 shows Success.
items.explain: The order is try, except, else. There was no error, so except is skipped and else runs. else always comes after except.

items.task: Put both input lines and the print of a / b inside try (leave the int() and input() parentheses empty). except ValueError prints “Numbers only”; except ZeroDivisionError prints “Can't divide by 0”. Example: 10 and 4 give 2.5
hints: There are three cases: normal, not a number, and dividing by 0. What's the output for each?
Write two excepts: one for ValueError and one for ZeroDivisionError.
Put both input lines and the division print inside try, and give each of the two excepts its own message.
items.explain: You gave each error its own except and message. You even got 0 as the first number right: that's no error, it just prints 0.0.

items.q: When does the else block run?
options: Only when try had no error
Only when there was an error
items.explain: else runs only when try finishes safely. The one that always runs, error or not, is finally.

LESSONS.title: Raising errors
LESSONS.goal: Raise your own errors and catch them with except
summary: raise ValueError("message")
A signal that the input is bad
Get the message with as e, then print(e)

cards.say: raise causes an error on purpose. Use it when the code is fine but the value makes no sense. Catch it with except ValueError as e: and the message in the parentheses ends up in e.
If a function raises an error, the code that called it can catch it with except. The function does the checking, the caller shows the message. Teamwork!

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: except ValueError catches a raised ValueError too. There's no e here, so the message isn't printed; only “Caught it” is.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: With as e, e holds the message from the parentheses. print(e) shows that message as it is.

items.q: What happens when you run this code?
items.code:
age = -5
if age < 0:
    raise ValueError("Bad age")
print("Passed")
options: A ValueError clue appears and it stops
items.explain: With no try to catch it, the raised error becomes a clue and the program stops. So “Passed” never shows up.

items.q: Fill in the blank so a negative price shows the message.
items.explain: ValueError is the right fit when a value makes no sense. With a different name, the except ValueError below can't catch it and you get the clue.

items.q: Put the lines in order so Done shows after the message.
items.explain: raise causes the error inside try, and except catches it and shows the message. The last print always runs.

items.task: Read an age with input() (leave the parentheses empty), convert it with int() and store it in age. If it's below 0, raise ValueError("Bad age"), then print(e) in except ValueError as e. Otherwise print “Age: N”. Example: 20 gives Age: 20
hints: The message only shows for values below 0; 0 itself is fine. Want to trace the example once?
Check with an if inside try, and raise an error if something's wrong. except is where it gets caught.
Inside try: the input, the negative check with raise, and the normal print. In except ValueError as e, print e.
items.explain: Only negative values raise an error, and except shows the message. You also got the edge right: 0 is not an error.

items.q: What does raise ValueError("…") do?
options: Causes an error on purpose, as a signal
Catches an error and removes it
Only checks whether there's an error
items.explain: raise is the side that makes errors. except is the side that catches them. Together they report bad input and deal with it.

LESSONS.title: Chapter 10 checkpoint
LESSONS.goal: Handle problems safely with try, except and raise
summary: Guess the cause from the clue's name
Specific excepts first, and always name the error
else runs on success; finally always runs

cards.say: Time to wrap up Chapter 10! Read the error's name, put only the errors you mean to catch in except, and raise your own when needed. Let's finish with a crash-proof calculator.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.code: print(int("3.5"))
items.explain: int() only converts strings shaped like whole numbers. "3.5" has the wrong shape, so it's a ValueError.

items.q: Which clue (error) do you get when you run this code?
items.code:
prices = {"milk": 1500}
print(prices["bread"])
items.explain: Asking for "bread", a key the dictionary doesn't have, gives a KeyError. With a list and a missing index, it would have been an IndexError.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: abc raises a ValueError, so A prints and else is skipped. C in finally always runs.

items.q: Fill in the blank so entering 0 shows the message.
items.explain: Dividing by 0 is a ZeroDivisionError. Other names can't catch it, so you'd get the clue.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: e holds the message from raise's parentheses. The comma in print shows it after the label.

items.q: Put the lines in order so entering -4 shows the message.
items.explain: Inside try, the order is input, check, raise; then except catches it. If the check came before the input, n wouldn't exist yet.

items.task: Inside try, read a, op and b with input() (a and b as int, empty parentheses). If op isn't "/", raise Exception("Unknown op"). ValueError prints “Please enter a number”, dividing by 0 prints “Can't divide by 0”, anything else does print(e). 9 / 2 gives 4.5
items.starter:
a = int(input())
op = input()
b = int(input())
hints: There are four cases: normal, not a number, dividing by 0, and an unknown operator. Jot down what each one prints.
Write three excepts. The two specific ones go first, and Exception goes last.
Read the inputs inside try, and raise if op isn't "/". If it is, print a / b. The last except uses as e.
items.explain: The specific ValueError and ZeroDivisionError come first, and the general Exception comes last. Passing the raised message through e works neatly too. In real code, a more specific error name than Exception is usually better.

items.q: Why is a bare except: with no error name risky?
options: It swallows every error and hides the cause
items.explain: A bare except swallows the clues from bugs you didn't expect too. Name the errors you catch, and the other clues survive.

ADVANCED.title: Making your own errors
ADVANCED.goal: Check values in your functions and raise the right error
summary: Put the bad value in an f-string message
TypeError for types, ValueError for values
The function checks; except shows the message

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. One step past raise from 10-4: let's put the bad value into the message with an f-string.

Pick the error type too. Wrong type of value → TypeError. Right type but the value makes no sense → ValueError. type(price) != int means “if price isn't an int”. Only the first check that fails gets raised. (Real code usually checks this with isinstance(price, int).)

items.q: If you enter -4, what's the output?
items.explain: The value -4 fills {n} in the f-string, so it's in the message. That message travels through e, and “Error: Can't order -4” is printed.

items.q: Which error fits when the type of the value itself is wrong?
items.explain: If an int should come in but something else arrives, like text, TypeError fits. Right type but a strange value is a ValueError.

items.q: If you enter 150, what's the output?
items.explain: 150 isn't below 0, so it passes the first check, but it's over 120, so the second check catches it. The moment that happens, raise leaves the function.

items.q: Fill in the blank after as so the message shows.
items.explain: The name after as is the label that receives the message. The code below does print(reason), so it must be reason. Any other name gives a NameError.

items.q: Put the lines in order so entering 0 shows the message.
items.explain: Check after reading the input, and raise if it fails. except catches it and prints e. If the check came first, n wouldn't exist yet.

items.task: Function check_qty(q): below 1, raise ValueError(f"Qty N is too small"); above 99, raise ValueError(f"N is too many"); otherwise return q. Inside try, call check_qty(int(input())), leaving input() empty; in except ValueError as e, print e. On success print “Order: N”. 3 → Order: 3
hints: There are three cases: below 1, above 99, and in between. Where do 99 and 1 go?
The checks and raise go inside the function; the except that shows the message goes where you call it. Remember 10-4.
Use two ifs inside the function, each with its own raise. Put the call inside try and catch it with except ValueError as e.
items.explain: The function checks and raises with the bad value in the message, and except shows it. The edges are right too: 1 and 99 pass, 0 and 100 get caught.

items.q: Why put the bad value in the message with an f-string?
options: You can see right away which value was the problem
items.explain: “Can't order 0” beats “Something's wrong”: when you can see the value, the cause is easy to find. You still need except, though.

ADVANCED.title: Re-raising errors
ADVANCED.goal: Know the order of raise inside except and finally
summary: A bare raise in except re-raises the same error
Log on the inside, handle on the outside
finally always runs just before leaving

cards.say: One more step! Let's combine except from 10-3 with raise from 10-4. A bare raise inside except throws the caught error again, unchanged. Log it on the inside, handle it on the outside.
cards.out:
Log: not a number
Handled outside

cards.say: finally always runs just before leaving the try statement, whether it leaves with return or, as here, by re-raising an error. That's why entering abc prints Log, Cleanup, then Outside.

items.q: If you enter 7, what's the output?
items.explain: Right before return 7 leaves, finally runs and prints “Cleanup”. Then the print outside shows the returned 7.

items.q: If you enter x, what's the output?
items.explain: except logs it and re-raises with raise. Just before the error leaves the function, finally does the cleanup, and then the outer except catches it.

items.q: If you enter x, what's the output?
items.explain: Without raise, the error ends in except. The function finishes with no value, so it returns None, and the outer except never runs.

items.q: Pick what goes in the blank so the outside handles it too.
items.explain: Only raise inside except throws the caught error again. pass does nothing, so the error never reaches the outside, and break outside a loop gives a clue.

items.q: If you enter 0, what's the output?
items.explain: Nested try works the same way. The inner except catches it first and prints “Inside”, then raise passes it on, and the outer try's except catches it next.

items.task: Write parse_age(text): in try, return int(text); in except ValueError, print “Log: not a number” and re-raise with a bare raise; in finally, print “Check done”. Outside, inside try, call parse_age(input()), leaving input() empty, and print “Age: N”; on error, print “Please try again”. 20 → Check done, Age: 20

tests.expect:
Log: not a number
Check done
Please try again

Log: not a number
Check done
Please try again

hints: Normal input shows Check done, then the age. An error shows the log, Check done, then Please try again.
The function's except only logs and re-raises the error. The outer try that called the function handles it.
Inside the function, write try, except ValueError and finally, with a bare raise at the end of except. Call the function from an outer try.
items.explain: The inside only logs and re-raises; the outside shows the message. You even got finally's timing right: “Check done” comes first, error or not.

items.q: When does the code inside finally run?
options: Always, even just before leaving with return or a re-raise
Only when except didn't catch the error
items.explain: finally runs just before leaving the try block, error or not. Same if you leave with return or re-raise with raise.

ADVANCED.title: Safe input
ADVANCED.goal: Ask again until valid, up to a limit
summary: The function checks; the loop asks again
Re-raise with your own message for clean output
A limit on tries means it always ends

cards.say: One more step: putting it to use. Remember asking again until it's right, back in 10-2? Let's add a range-checking function. Not a number, or out of range? We ask again.
Instead of int()'s long technical message, raise your own short one for a cleaner result. Limit the tries with for so it doesn't ask forever. On success, break out.

items.q: If you enter 0 and then 5, what's the output?
items.explain: 0 is below 1, so it asks again. 5 is the top of the range, so it passes. Then break leaves the loop and “5 stars” is printed.

items.q: If you enter x, what's the output?
items.explain: Raising with a new message inside except puts your message in e. A bare raise would have kept int()'s own long message.

items.q: Fill it in so the loop ends once a valid number comes in.
items.explain: You need break to leave the for loop on success. With pass or continue, the next round calls input() again and you get a clue.

items.q: If you enter a, b and c in turn, what's the output?
items.explain: All three raise a ValueError, so “Again” prints three times. None succeeded, so ok stays False and “Gave up” shows at the end.

items.task: Function ask_star(text): if it's not a number, raise ValueError("Not an int"); if it's outside 1-5, raise ValueError("Not 1-5"); otherwise return the int. Call it in try with input() (empty parentheses), up to 3 times. On failure print e; on success print “Stars: N” and stop. If all 3 fail, print “Gave up”. 4 → Stars: 4

tests.expect:
Not 1-5
Not 1-5
Not an int
Gave up

hints: Stop on success; give up after 3 misses. 1 and 5 succeed, 0 and 6 fail.
Checks and raise go in the function, the number of tries comes from for, and asking again uses try and except. Remember 10-2 and 10-A1.
Keep one variable that says whether you succeeded. After the loop, if it doesn't say success, print the give-up message.
items.explain: The function checks and raises with your message, and the loop shows it and asks again. The 3-try limit, the give-up message and the edges 1 and 5 are all right.

items.q: Why give an ask-again loop a maximum number of tries?
options: So it can end instead of asking forever
items.explain: Without a limit, input that's always wrong could keep it going forever. With a limit, it wraps up with a give-up message.

TEMPLATES.q: We try to turn text that isn't a number into an int. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.explain: If int() can't convert it, you get a ValueError. except ValueError catches it and prints the message. TypeError is a different kind of error, so it can't catch this.

TEMPLATES.q: We want to catch the divide-by-zero error. Fill in the blank.
TEMPLATES.explain: Dividing by 0 raises a ZeroDivisionError. except only catches it if the name matches. With another name, the error isn't caught and you get the clue.

TEMPLATES.q: There are two excepts. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.explain: nums[5] is out of range, so it raises an IndexError. The except that matches the error runs. With no matching except, the error isn't caught and you get the clue.

TEMPLATES.q: This function blocks negative ages. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.explain: The text you raise with ValueError(text) lands in e in except … as e. print(e) shows that text. "e" in quotes is just the letter e.

TEMPLATES.q: If it's not a number, we'll treat it as 0 and keep calculating. Fill in the blank.
TEMPLATES.explain: Putting the number 0 into n inside except lets the calculation continue. "0" is a string and None is no value at all, so adding to either causes an error.
